I farm 8 mu in a wheat-maize rotation, so I will treat the same 8 mu as winter wheat land and then summer maize land. I do not start from zero. I will begin from what has worked for me in recent years and only adjust a little. With well irrigation, I can push yield more steadily than dryland, so I will not underfeed the crop. Fertilizer costs money, but losing yield costs more, especially on wheat and maize where income depends on stable output. Since I have high education and have farmed 20 years, I look at the field more systematically: soil moisture, stand density, fertilizer balance, and whether last year there was lodging, weak tillering, or poor grain filling.

For winter wheat, I will use improved seed again, not old saved seed. Wheat here responds well to base fertilizer plus topdressing, and with irrigation I can support a stronger stand. I will keep nitrogen a bit on the safe side because weak wheat is hard to fix later. I will put most phosphorus and potassium in as base fertilizer, then split nitrogen between sowing and spring jointing. I will irrigate about 3 times if water conditions are normal: once for overwintering if the soil is dry, once at jointing, and once around booting or grain filling. For pests and disease, I will plan 3 sprays because one cheap missed spray can cost more than the chemical bill. For tillage, after maize I will use rotary tillage because on my scale it is efficient and gives me a clean wheat seedbed without the heavier cost of ploughing every year.

For summer maize, I will use hybrid seed. In my area, hybrid maize gives me more confidence on yield and ear size, and most serious growers around me use it. After wheat harvest, time is tight, so I will keep maize establishment simple and efficient. I will use no-tillage planting into wheat stubble if the machine is available, because it saves time and protects moisture. I will not push maize fertilizer as high as wheat, but I will still feed it enough to avoid thin stalks and short ears. I will usually give 2 irrigations if rainfall is normal: one around the big flare stage and one around silking or grain fill if the field needs it. For pesticide, I will plan 2 applications, mainly for weeds early and then for insects or leaf disease later if pressure shows up. On 8 mu, I still count every yuan, but I will spend where the yield return is dependable.
